summary: An agent stops and asks before doing something consequential, and a person approves, rejects or edits it.
useWhen: the action spends money, sends something to a third party, deletes data, or changes access
the action is irreversible by the person who would have to undo it
a regulation or an internal policy requires a human decision on the record — the EU AI Act's human-oversight duty is the common case
structure: The gate appears in place, where the run reached it — inside the step log, not in a dialog that covers it.
The AgentActivityStep that is waiting stays `active`; the ApprovalGate is its `detail`.
An ApprovalGate whose `title` names the action and its object, with the specifics — amount, recipient, record count — as `children`.
`risk` set from the consequence, not from the agent's confidence.
After the decision, `status` becomes `approved`, `rejected` or `expired` and `resolution` records who decided and when.

loading.must: While the decision is being submitted, set `isSubmitting` — the gate keeps its buttons in place and disables them. Do not remove the gate or advance the step log until the server confirms.
loading.why: an optimistically-advanced run tells the user the action was approved before anything approved it, which is the one thing this pattern exists to prevent

empty.must: Render no ApprovalGate when nothing is waiting. A queue view with no pending items says so in words and does not render an empty gate shell.
empty.why: a gate with no action in it still shows Approve and Reject buttons, and a user who presses one has approved nothing while believing they approved something

error.must: If the decision fails to submit, keep `status="pending"`, clear `isSubmitting`, and show an Alert with `intent="error"` inside the gate. The action must not proceed.
error.why: a failed approval that looks like a successful one is an unapproved action running with a human's name on it

expired.must: Set `status="expired"` when the window closes, state what happened by default in `resolution`, and remove the decision buttons.
expired.why: a gate that sits pending forever hides that the agent already gave up, and buttons that no longer do anything are worse than no buttons

requires: a `title` that names the action and the object — it is the gate's accessible name
`risk` set from consequence, so the level is the same for the same action every time
reject reachable before approve by keyboard, which the component's DOM order already guarantees
notes: ApprovalGate autofocuses nothing, deliberately. A dialog that focuses Approve turns Enter on an unread screen into consent.
Do not put the gate in a Modal that traps focus and hides the run behind it. The evidence for the decision is the step log, and a person cannot judge an action they can no longer see.
`risk` is a label on the consequence, not a colour scheme. Using `high` for emphasis on a routine action is how a team learns to ignore it.

antiPatterns.why: it names neither the action nor its object, so the only available answer is a reflex — and a reflex is not oversight

antiPatterns.dont: an approval that also acts as the progress indicator
antiPatterns.why: conflating "I am working" with "I need you" teaches the user to dismiss both

antiPatterns.dont: approve-all across a queue of unrelated actions
antiPatterns.why: one click covering many consequences is indistinguishable from no gate at all, and it is the failure regulators look for

antiPatterns.dont: a countdown that approves on expiry
antiPatterns.why: silence is not consent; an expired gate must default to the safe outcome, which is not doing the thing

antiPatterns.dont: hiding the gate's earlier steps once a decision is made
antiPatterns.why: the record of what was approved, on what evidence, is the artefact an audit asks for
